title: Specht v. Netscape Communications Corp.
summary: Downloading free software did not manifest assent to license terms hidden below the download button without reasonably conspicuous notice.

sections.Parties: Users sued Netscape and its corporate parent over SmartDownload’s alleged transmission of information about their downloads. Netscape sought to require arbitration under software license terms.
sections.Material Facts:
The website offered both Communicator and SmartDownload. Installing Communicator displayed its license and required clicking “Yes”; users could not complete installation otherwise. That agreement did not mention SmartDownload. SmartDownload, by contrast, could be downloaded immediately through a prominent button. The only reference to its license appeared below that button on a part of the page a user would see only by scrolling.

Even a user who scrolled would first encounter a prompt to review the license and would then need to follow links to another page. The users denied knowing about SmartDownload’s terms. Netscape did not refute that testimony. A visible scrollbar showed that more material existed below, but did not itself identify that material as contract terms.
sections.Procedural History: The Southern District of New York denied the motion to compel arbitration and stay the actions. The Second Circuit affirmed under the California contract-formation law used by the district court and not challenged on appeal. The assigned excerpt focuses on assent to SmartDownload’s license rather than all issues discussed in the full opinion.
sections.Issue: Did the act of downloading constitute agreement to the arbitration provision when a reasonably prudent user would not have encountered notice of the license before downloading?
sections.Holding: No. Reasonably conspicuous notice and an unambiguous manifestation of assent were absent in the circumstances presented.
sections.Reasoning:
The objective inquiry includes the surrounding transaction and the design through which a claimed acceptance occurs. A person who signs an apparent contract ordinarily has reason to examine its terms. A person responding to an invitation to download free software is not necessarily alerted to contractual provisions hidden outside the visible invitation. The duty to read does not answer the prior question whether the recipient received reasonable notice that terms were being proposed.

The Communicator installation illustrated a materially different process: it displayed terms and required affirmative agreement. Acceptance of that separate license did not make the hidden SmartDownload terms part of the users’ agreement. The court also rejected the argument that noticing an unfinished webpage creates inquiry notice of any possible legal terms below.

Arbitration depends on an agreement, and the policy favoring arbitration does not supply missing assent. The result does not prohibit electronic contracting or make a mouse click ineffective. It identifies how a click’s meaning depends on the notice and choice presented to the user at that point.

sections.Parties: Software users sued Netscape and AOL; the defendants sought arbitration.
sections.Material Facts: The reference to SmartDownload’s terms appeared below the download button, outside the initially visible screen. Users could download without seeing those terms.
sections.Procedural History: The Southern District of New York denied the motion to compel arbitration and stay the action. The Second Circuit affirmed.
sections.Issue: Had the users assented to the SmartDownload arbitration provision through the downloading process?
sections.Holding: No, under the circumstances and governing contract law analyzed.
sections.Reasoning: The court required reasonably conspicuous notice and an unambiguous manifestation of assent. It assessed what a reasonably prudent offeree would have known before clicking.

priorVersions.summary: Downloading SmartDownload did not show assent to terms whose existence was not reasonably brought to the users’ attention.
priorVersions.notes:
Court: Second Circuit (2002).

The casebook distinguishes assent to a transaction from adoption of a particular embedded term. Communicator’s affirmative acceptance procedure and SmartDownload’s inconspicuous notice must not be conflated. Later online cases beginning at p. 304 are only partially within the present assignment.

sections.Parties: Users of Netscape software sued Netscape and related defendants over alleged collection of electronic information. Netscape sought arbitration under software terms.
sections.Material Facts: The interface for SmartDownload displayed a download button without presenting the contractual notice above it. A user needed to scroll below the initially visible page to find a notice, then follow links to locate terms. The separate Communicator program involved an affirmative clickwrap mechanism. The existence of that separate agreement did not itself establish assent to the SmartDownload terms at issue.
sections.Procedural History: The district court denied the motion to compel arbitration. The Second Circuit affirmed under the applicable state-law contract analysis. The decision concerns agreement to arbitrate, not the merits of the users’ statutory privacy claims.
sections.Issue: Did pressing the download button unambiguously manifest assent when a reasonably prudent user would not have encountered notice of the license terms before downloading?
sections.Holding: No. Reasonably conspicuous notice of the terms and an unambiguous manifestation of assent were lacking for the disputed SmartDownload agreement.
sections.Reasoning: The objective approach considers the transactional interface through which conduct takes on meaning. A download can communicate a desire for software without communicating agreement to a hidden contract. A scroll bar alone does not alert a user that contractual terms lie below the button. The duty to read presupposes adequate notice that contractual terms are being offered; it does not make every remotely accessible page binding. The opinion preserves the possibility of effective online assent under a different design.

sources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 178–183. Open assigned page 178.

learning.why: Specht explains why notice must precede a meaningful inference of assent. It connects directly to Hill, Klocek, Klar, and the later assigned Anderson decision, despite their different procedural settings.

topics.assent: The download action did not communicate agreement to undisclosed terms.
topics.notice: The page layout did not give reasonable notice before the action.
topics.standard-forms: The case distinguishes agreeing to a transaction from accepting a particular standardized term.
topics.arbitration: The threshold question was whether an agreement to arbitrate existed.
topics.objective-assent: Objective interpretation considers the interface and transactional setting.

mnemonic.rationale: Terms hidden below the download button
